source: Brooks (1983) Towards a theory of the comprehension of computer programs (as described in von Mayrhauser & Vans (1995) Program comprehension during software maintenance and evolution)
finding: Comprehension is top-down reconstruction of the mapping from the problem domain to code through intermediate domains. A first vague primary hypothesis is refined into subsidiary hypotheses until each can be matched to code. Hypotheses are the only drivers of cognition. Beacons are used to verify them.
numbers: Understanding is complete when the mental model holds a full hierarchy of hypotheses. Example chain of domains: inventory, accounting, mathematics, programming language (4 domains).
quote: Brooks theorizes that hypotheses are the only drivers of cognition.
limits: Read via the 1995 review, not the 1983 paper. The knowledge structures are left undefined (the review's critique).
agent_relevance: Gives a clean hypothesis-tree episode type: generate hypothesis, look for beacon, confirm, refine or reject. Fits the schema's check-before-trust rules.

source: Brooks (1978, 1983) as traced by Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model
finding: Brooks (1978) first said understanding is successive refinement of hypotheses. The 1983 paper made it the top-down model and named code cues 'beacons' for the first time. Long time on one snippet is read as trouble finding a right hypothesis.
numbers: No participant numbers in the history.
limits: Secondary history. The author notes most studies define comprehension by their own task, so measures differ across studies.
agent_relevance: A long stall on a block is a signal of a failed hypothesis; the agent can use it as a trigger to name a new hypothesis.

source: Shneiderman & Mayer (1979) Syntactic/semantic interactions in programmer behavior, as quoted in Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model
finding: Bottom-up model: programmers recode code into a multilevel internal semantic structure by chunking statements, then chunking chunks, instead of memorising line by line. Long-term memory holds syntactic (language-bound) and semantic (language-free) knowledge.
numbers: Five programming tasks were studied; one was comprehension.
quote: programmers recognize the function of groups of statements, and then piece together these chunks to form even larger chunks
limits: Read via Wyrich and the 1995 review. Original sample sizes not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports reading episodes labelled as chunk-then-summarise steps, one summary line per block.

source: Soloway & Ehrlich (1984) Empirical studies of programming knowledge, as described in von Mayrhauser & Vans (1995) Program comprehension during software maintenance and evolution
finding: Experts hold programming plans and rules of discourse. Experts do much better on plan-like code than on unplan-like code, so unconventional style hurts even experts. Top-down understanding works when code is familiar.
numbers: Exact percent-correct and N were not obtained this session. The review says only 'significantly better'.
limits: Primary paper not opened (PDF host blocked). Numbers must be pulled from the 1984 TSE paper before use.
agent_relevance: Rules of discourse (names match function, no dead code, a tested condition can be true) can become cheap code checks that flag surprising code for a closer read.

source: Pennington (1987) Stimulus structures and mental representations in expert comprehension of computer programs (as described in von Mayrhauser & Vans (1995) Program comprehension during software maintenance and evolution and Burkhardt et al. 1997)
finding: Two representations. The program model (control flow, elementary operations) forms first and bottom-up from beacons. The situation model (data flow, function, goal hierarchy) forms later. Procedural units, not functional ones, were the base of expert memory for new code.
numbers: Paradigm: read a program for limited time, then answer questions per information category. A search snippet says Study 1 tested 80 professional programmers on comprehension and recognition (not verified in text).
limits: Procedural languages and short programs. Not opened as primary. The OO replication (Burkhardt et al.) found a different order.
agent_relevance: For unfamiliar code the agent should first build a control-flow trace, then the function and goal story.

source: Letovsky (1987) Cognitive processes in program comprehension (as described in von Mayrhauser & Vans (1995) Program comprehension during software maintenance and evolution and Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model)
finding: Knowledge-based understander with a knowledge base, a mental model (specification, implementation and annotation layers) and an assimilation process. Conjectures come as why, how and what questions with graded certainty. Dangling purposes are unresolved goal-to-code links.
numbers: Data: think-aloud video of six professional programmers adding a feature.
quote: is best viewed as an opportunistic processor capable of exploiting both bottom-up and top-down cues as they become available
limits: Six people, one task type. Journal date is 1987 though often cited as 1986.
agent_relevance: The best fit for our episode labels: each episode is a question (why/how/what), a conjecture, and a verification with a certainty level. Open dangling purposes can be tracked as a list.

source: Littman, Pinto, Letovsky & Soloway (1986/87) as described in Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model
finding: Programmers using a systematic strategy (symbolic execution of data-flow paths between routines) built strong mental models (static plus causal knowledge) and did better at the modification task. Those using an as-needed strategy built weak models.
numbers: Counts not given in the secondary source.
limits: Secondary. Koenemann & Robertson (1991) later found as-needed reading is common and goal-driven, with bottom-up used when hypotheses fail.
agent_relevance: Evidence that for change tasks causal tracing beats skimming. Supports a forced data-flow trace before edits.

source: Wiedenbeck (1986) Beacons in computer program comprehension, as described in Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model
finding: Two experiments: code cues (beacons) help experienced programmers mainly and matter less to inexperienced ones. Beacons link top-down hypotheses to program text.
numbers: Sample sizes not given in the secondary source.
limits: Secondary. The beacon effect was not found in the 2017 fMRI study, and LLMs overweight names (see lexical superstition line).
agent_relevance: Identifier names are a cue to use but not to trust.

source: von Mayrhauser & Vans (1995) Program comprehension during software maintenance and evolution
finding: Integrated metamodel: top-down model (Soloway), program model and situation model (Pennington), plus a knowledge base. Programmers switch between all three. Chunking and cross-referencing are the two mechanisms. Comprehension is opportunistic, not one fixed direction.
numbers: Compares six models. Experiment census (Table 4): mostly observational studies on small programs (under 900 LOC); few on medium (900-40,000) or large code.
limits: Authors say most models assume the goal is to understand all code, not partial understanding such as debugging. Scale-up from small programs is open.
agent_relevance: The agent needs a switch rule between top-down (familiar code) and bottom-up (new code). Switching only on a failed hypothesis matches G1.

source: Busjahn, Bednarik, Begel, Crosby, Paterson, Schulte, Sharif, Tamm (2015) Eye movements in code reading: relaxing the linear order (ICPC)
finding: Novices read code less linearly than prose, and experts read it less linearly than novices. Experts jump further, cover fewer elements, and follow execution order more than story (top-to-bottom) order.
numbers: 14 novices (Java course) and 6 professionals. Novices: about 80% linear eye moves on text, 70% on code; experts about 60% on code. Saccade length 1.86 deg novices vs 3.12 deg experts (U=105, p<0.001). Code elements fixated: 52.42% novices vs 41.27% experts (U=84, p<0.01). Novice element coverage text 83.46% vs code 60.38% (W=21, p=0.03). Naive story-order alignment score novices -73.47 vs experts -161.52.
quote: novices read source code less linearly than they read English text
limits: Very small expert group. Novice programs were mostly linear in execution, so higher novice execution-order similarity is partly an artifact.
agent_relevance: Experts skip to what matters. An agent reading code in file order behaves like a novice; the reading plan should follow call or execution order.

source: Peitek, Siegmund & Apel (2020) What drives the reading order of programmers? (ICPC)
finding: Non-exact replication of Busjahn and Peachock. Experience changes reading (agreeing with Busjahn, not Peachock), but how linear the code itself is has a bigger effect. Comprehension strategy (top-down vs bottom-up) has a minor effect.
numbers: 12 novices and 19 intermediate programmers. Correctness 86% vs 91% (U=11121, p=0.072). Intermediates were faster overall (65 s vs 83 s, p<0.001); with meaningful names 55 s vs 76 s (p<0.001). FDR-adjusted threshold p<0.033. Source-code linearity affected nearly every measure (p=0.000). Busjahn's N-W story-order difference between experience groups was NOT reproduced (non-significant). Peachock found no experience effect on any measure (p 0.41 to 0.97).
quote: linearity of source code has an even stronger effect on reading order than experience
limits: 'Experts' were intermediate programmers. Linearity categories A to E confound with snippet content. Saccade length and N-W scores were not monotone with code linearity.
agent_relevance: Reading order is driven mostly by the code's own jump structure, so a reading-strategy label without code context misleads. Do not rely on one eye-tracking study when defining episode labels.

source: Peitek, Siegmund & Apel (2020), compiler-error side result
finding: Three obfuscated snippets accidentally contained an undefined variable. Most intermediate programmers missed it; many novices noticed it. This fits Shneiderman and Mayer: experts read for meaning, novices read symbols.
numbers: Counts per group are in a table that the text extraction garbled, so no figures are given here.
limits: Anecdotal. Three intermediate programmers confirmed in interviews that IDE highlighting normally catches this.
agent_relevance: Semantic reading can hide surface errors. A model reading for meaning will miss typos and undefined names; pair it with a compiler or lint pass.

source: Burkhardt, Detienne & Wiedenbeck (1997) Mental representations constructed by experts and novices in object-oriented program comprehension
finding: Tests Pennington's program-versus-situation model on OO code. The situation model was better than the program model and stronger for experts. The program model did not differ by expertise. The situation model improved after a real task; the program model did not. This contradicts Pennington's program-model-first order for OO code.
numbers: Situation mean 4.36 vs program mean 3.55 (max 6; F(1,43)=110.94, p<.0001). Experts 4.56 vs novices 4.10 on situation model (F(1,44)=19.17, p<.0001). Phase 1 to phase 2 on situation 4.17 to 4.55 (F=10.83, p<.002). Static info 4.74 vs dynamic 3.62 (p<.0001). About 46 subjects (inferred from F degrees of freedom).
limits: One OO program (a database). The authors suggest the OO paradigm may help build the situation model early.
agent_relevance: A boundary condition: with well-named objects the goal story may come first, so trace-first is not universal.

source: Siegmund, Peitek, Parnin, Apel et al. (2017) Measuring neural efficiency of program comprehension (ESEC/FSE)
finding: fMRI replication of the 2014 bottom-up study. The same left-hemisphere areas (BA 6, 21, 40, 44, 47) were active for bottom-up reading. Comprehension from semantic cues needed less activation everywhere, and BA 39 (a semantic integration hub) was off. This supports chunking in bottom-up reading and efficiency when hypotheses guide reading.
numbers: 11 participants (5 CS students, 3 maths students, 3 professionals; mean experience 1.7 years), 14 sessions. Threshold p<0.01 FDR. Cue-based reading showed lower activation than bottom-up in every area tested.
limits: Cue-based reading was primed by training on near-identical snippets, so it may reflect recognition rather than comprehension (authors' caveat). Small N.
agent_relevance: Familiar-pattern reading is cheap and bottom-up chunking is costly. Spend heavy tracing only on unfamiliar blocks.

source: Siegmund et al. (2017), beacon and layout null result
finding: No effect of beacons or layout on brain activation. The authors say the role of beacons may differ from older claims.
numbers: No significant differences among the 4 semantic-cue conditions (beacons present or absent x pretty-printed or disrupted layout).
limits: Authors blame the design (too little demand after training) rather than disproving beacons.
agent_relevance: Do not build rules that treat beacon presence alone as proof of understanding.

source: Goncalves, Rani, Storey, Spinellis & Bacchelli (2025) Code review comprehension: reviewing strategies seen through code comprehension theories (ICPC 2025)
finding: Applying Letovsky's model to real code review, reviewers used opportunistic strategies. Most began with a context-building phase, then code inspection (reading, testing), then discussion. Review scope varied: full, aspect-focused, partial or shallow.
numbers: 10 experienced reviewers, 25 reviews (15 open source, 10 closed source), think-aloud plus interviews. In 23 reviews the sequence began with context building and then inspection.
limits: Qualitative and small. Reviewers were recommended as great reviewers, so skewed to expert behaviour.
agent_relevance: Concrete episode vocabulary: context build, inspect, test, discuss; plus a scope label so the agent states how deep it went.

source: Zhang, Zhang, Leach & Huang (2026) EyeLayer: integrating human attention patterns into LLM-based code summarization (ICPC 2026)
finding: A small module learned from human gaze, added to four LLMs, improved code summaries on every metric. Gains were largest for small or less supervised models.
numbers: 625 eye-tracking samples from 27 professional developers (64 unique Java functions). BLEU-4: Llama3.2-1B 14.31 to 16.18; 3B 15.64 to 16.86; Qwen3-1.7B 13.36 to 15.12 (13.17% relative); Qwen3-4B 15.24 to 17.22. Layer 13 insertion helped; layer 4 hurt.
limits: Metrics are overlap with human summaries, not tests of understanding. Small gaze set, Java only.
agent_relevance: Weak support that expert attention can help. It needs training, which we do not do; the scaffold analogue is choosing which lines the agent reads first.

source: Li, Zhang, Karas, McMillan, Leach & Huang (2024) Do machines and humans focus on similar code? (ICPC 2024)
finding: Negative result. Perturbation-based (SHAP) focus of six code models showed no meaningful link to where 27 programmers looked while summarizing code. Focus alignment did not predict summary quality.
numbers: 671 human trials, 68 Java methods. Only 22% of methods had a significant human-machine Spearman correlation (human duration vs fixation: 85%). Significant rho clustered near +0.5 or -0.5. Alignment vs summary quality: rho = -0.1279, p = 0.3862 (one row of Table 2; metric not confirmed). Models weighted comments, literals and assignments more; humans weighted method calls and external names more.
limits: SHAP on black-box models may not reflect real attention. Paltenghi et al. reportedly found CodeGen attention did align (secondhand).
agent_relevance: Do not assume an LLM reads code like a person. Put human-like reading steps into the scaffold instead of hoping for them.

source: Shen, Xi, Du & Li (2026) On the lexical superstition of LLMs for code comprehension
finding: LLMs lean too heavily on identifier names. When names are removed or made misleading, performance falls and answers follow the misleading name. Prompt and fine-tune fixes did not remove it.
numbers: Code completion Pass@1 with misleading names fell 16.97% to 34.18% relative across four LLMs (LLaMA3-70B 62.20 to 40.94). Code-document selection, GPT-3.5-turbo: 92.84% original, 52.39% with confusing names (near chance), 81.35% anonymous (-12.37%). Type inference, where the answer is locally recoverable, showed smaller naming effects.
limits: Preprint under review. Names are often useful in real code; the authors call this a vulnerability, not a rejection of names.
agent_relevance: The LLM counterpart of the beacon effect. Add a rename-and-recheck step: re-read the block with names masked and see whether the explanation holds.

source: Le, Nguyen & Nguyen (2026) Do machines struggle where humans do? LLM and human comprehension of obfuscated code
finding: Reasoning-tuned small models track which obfuscated tasks humans find hard; coder and instruct models do not. Human experts did better under moderate obfuscation (they use structure); models did not copy that.
numbers: Spearman rho with human accuracy: Qwen3-0.6B 0.30, Phi-4 Mini 0.47, SmolLM3-3B 0.36, DS-R1-Qwen-7B 0.37 (all p<0.01); Llama-3.1-8B 0.08, CodeLlama-7B 0.02, DS-Coder-6.7B 0.10 (not significant). Output-prediction accuracy at no obfuscation: DS-R1-Qwen-7B 64% vs coder models 9 to 13%. Five obfuscation tiers, Python and JavaScript, two task sets.
limits: Models are 0.6B to 8B only. Human data reused from an earlier study. Alignment is not accuracy: the best-aligned model was a weak performer.
agent_relevance: Reasoning mode matters for comprehension-like tasks; supports a forced trace step. Chain-of-thought length tracked task difficulty.

source: Rong, Yadavally, Dhulipala, Nguyen & Nguyen (2026) Behavioral alignment of model-code and human-code understandability via behavioral proxies (ISSTA 2026)
finding: LLM judgements of code understandability align best with professional developers and less with students. Role prompts for student readers did not help. Self-consistency of intent summaries is a usable proxy for model understandability.
numbers: Binary classification against human-rated understandability; closed models 72.2 to 72.7 F1 on the reviewer proxy, open models 25.9 to 72.6. In 19.3% of cases bachelor's students believed they understood a snippet but answered at most one comprehension question right.
limits: Preprint. Labels skewed toward the positive class.
agent_relevance: The agent cannot be steered to read like a novice by role prompts. Self-consistency of summaries of one block could serve as an uncertainty signal, with the G4 caution.

source: Wyrich (2023), comparability of comprehension measures
finding: Different comprehension measures (questions, recall, time, correctness) mostly do not correlate with each other. Each study defines comprehension by its own task, so results are hard to compare.
numbers: Cites comparability studies (refs 2, 7, 16, 23, 69) that overwhelmingly found low agreement.
limits: Secondary statement; underlying coefficients not opened.
agent_relevance: Judge comprehension by a task (predict output, locate fault), not by self-report.

source: Gilmore (1991) as quoted in Wyrich (2023) Source code comprehension: a contemporary definition and conceptual model: comprehension inside debugging
finding: Comprehension is part of a larger debugging loop, not a separate step that builds a model first and then debugs.
numbers: No numbers in the quote.
limits: Secondary. Original not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports interleaving reading and test runs instead of reading everything before running anything.

source: Maletic slides: Mental models for program understanding (Kent State)
finding: Teaching summary: a mental model of a system is needed to use or modify it, and how deep it must be depends on the goal. Example: driving versus fixing a car.
numbers: None.
limits: Slides, low authority, no data.
agent_relevance: Reading depth should scale with the task goal; set a scope label per task.

source: Kevic et al. (2015) Tracing software developers' eyes and interactions for change tasks, as cited in a lecture slide set (search result)
finding: Developers fixate on only a small part of the lines in a method and follow data flow inside the method.
numbers: Search snippet: on average 32% of lines in a method were looked at; 58% of navigations stayed within the slice. Unverified.
limits: Not opened. Figures come from a search snippet of a slide deck.
agent_relevance: Targeted reading along slices instead of whole files. Check the source before use.

source: Schroeder & Koschke (2024) Recording and interpreting developer behaviour in programming tasks (IDE workshop)
finding: The paper notes that models of top-down and bottom-up comprehension seem incomplete: the patterns they predict were not observed in recorded IDE behaviour. The authors use abstracted action patterns of file visits and edits instead.
numbers: Three studies with the MIMESIS plug-in; no effect sizes were extracted from the pages read.
limits: Only the abstract, introduction and related work were read. Short, exploratory.
agent_relevance: Classic theories predict real IDE behaviour less well than they look; keep episode labels data-driven.

source: ICSE 2025 journal-first: A tale of two comprehensions - student attention during code summarization (search result)
finding: Eye tracking compares reading code that already has a summary with writing a summary. Finds attention differences between the tasks, similar reading patterns, and demographic effects.
numbers: Search snippet: n = 27 students.
limits: Abstract level only, not opened.
agent_relevance: Reading for a task (write a summary) changes what is attended to; set the reading goal first.
